newsitem.title: UK: BBC transmission sale to raise 244 million pounds.
newsitem.headline: BBC transmission sale to raise 244 million pounds.

text.p: The BBC said Thursday it would complete the sale Friday of its domestic radio and television transmission business to a U.S.-led consortium for 244 million pounds ($397 million).
The unit is being bought by Castle Transmission Services, a consortium headed by Houston-based Castle Tower Corp.

The BBC announced last month that the consortium had been selected as the preferred bidder but the actual sale price is above what had been forecast. Most financial analysts had been expecting the deal to raise little over 200 million pounds ($325 million).

The state-owned BBC, which derives the bulk of its funding from an annual levy payable by television set owners, will use the proceeds from the sale to help pay for new services in the multi-channel digital era.

"When the government set BBC Transmission on the road to privatisation, we were determined that our interests and those of our license payers would be protected with guarantees on both quality and cost," said BBC Deputy Director-General Bob Phillis.
"We are delighted that in Castle we have found a purchaser who best satisfied those criteria as well as offering excellent financial terms," he added.
Castle Tower, the consortium's managing partner, operates more than 1,200 wireless and broadcast communication sites throughout the United States and the Caribbean.
Its partners include Telediffusion de France, part of the France Telecom Group, plus investment firms Berkshire Partners LLC and Candover Investments Plc .
The Castle consortium has been granted a 10-year contract for transmission of BBC1 and BBC2 analogue television services and the BBC's five national radio stations.

Assets included in the sale include freeholds and leaseholds on nearly 740 transmitter sites across Britain and related equipment. Under the terms of the deal, 500 BBC staff will transfer to the new company.
The cash injection is a welcome boost to the BBC, which is planning to offer all license payers supplementary digital television channels, including a 24-hour news station.
The British government recently rejected the BBC's demand for an increase in the licence fee above the inflation rate. It came up with a five-year formula which maintained the link to prices.
